title: Coherent quantum control of dark excitons in hybrid metal organic chalchogenolates
authors: Christian L. McCoy, Tobias Saule, Mariya Aleksich, Maggie C. Willson, J. Nathan Hohman, Thomas Weinacht, George N. Gibson, Carlos A. Trallero-Herrero
abstract: Artificial atom-like systems are a promising candidate for next generation quantum processing. Among them, dark excitons exhibit one of the longest lifetimes at high temperatures. Here, we demonstrate coherent control of dark excitonic states in metal-organic chalcogenolates (MOChas) by using an ultrafast pulse shaper at room temperature. These dark exciton states are optically accessed via two-photon absorption and directly read out with a four-wave mixing process. The system is described by a non-perturbative, two-photon Hamiltonian based on well-known atomic physics and applied to a three level system comprised of two dark excitons. Empirical and theoretical state specific optical access is shown via a simple optical pulse shape. The developed Hamiltonian-based description is a first step towards a quantum processing platform using three-level systems and two photon transitions, one example being dark excitons in the MOCha silver benzeneselenolate (mithrene). Simple conditions for gate operations are laid out and described.
summary: The research demonstrates coherent quantum control of dark excitons—optically forbidden excited states—in MOChas at room temperature. By employing ultrafast pulse shaping and probing the system via Four-Wave Mixing, the authors show they can manipulate these states using a derived Hamiltonian model. This work establishes a solid-state platform for realizing fundamental quantum gate operations.
main_problem: The goal is to demonstrate coherent quantum control over dark exciton states within Metal-Organic Chalcogenolates (MOChas) for use in next-generation quantum processing platforms.
main_result: Coherent control was successfully demonstrated using ultrafast pulse shaping at room temperature, confirming the feasibility of using these solid-state systems for implementing basic quantum gate operations.
method: The study combines theoretical modeling using a non-perturbative Hamiltonian with experimental techniques like Four-Wave Mixing (FWM) and ultrafast pulse shaping.
model_or_system: The physical system is dark excitons in MOChas, modeled by a three-level system described by a two-photon Hamiltonian. The control mechanism relies on tailoring the spectral phase of an ultrafast laser pulse to manipulate state populations.
key_observables: FWM emission energy, which reveals resonance structure; the achievable quantum gate operations (e.g., $\pi/2$ rotation) characterized by pulse areas ($	heta$).
important_parameters: Room temperature operation, two-photon absorption access, and the ability to tune detuning ($\delta(t)$) relative to coupling strengths ($\chi(t)$).
main_assumptions: The initial theoretical description is limited to the perturbative regime, and the model simplifies by neglecting certain state couplings.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the excitonic state diagram (single-photon vs. two-photon allowed), the FWM experimental setup using a pulse shaper, and energy maps showing resonance features dependent on phase jumps.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical system and its limitations to developing a Hamiltonian description, demonstrating control via ultrafast spectroscopy measurements (FWM scans), and finally outlining the theoretical requirements for implementing quantum gates.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges solid-state physics with quantum information science by showing how engineered excitonic states in organic semiconductors can be manipulated coherently using tailored light fields, mimicking atomic quantum control schemes.
